name: Maragathachaleswarar Temple, Tiruveengoimalai
deity: Shiva as Maragathachaleswarar (Eengoinathar), with the goddess Marakathavalli
period: Ancient Shaiva hill shrine of Chola Nadu, sung by Sambandar in the Tevaram (7th century); stone temple of the Chola era with later additions
dynasty: Early medieval Tamil patrons (Chola-era stone rebuilding and later)
summary: Maragathachaleswarar is the emerald-hill shrine of Tiruveengoimalai, a Tevaram temple praised by Sambandar, set on a small rock north of the Kaveri and remembered for the legend of a fragment of the cosmic mountain that fell here and became an emerald linga.

sections.history: Tiruveengoimalai lies in Tiruchirappalli district, on the northern side of the Kaveri, among the old Shaiva shrines of the Chola country. The saint Sambandar praised it in a decad of verses in the Tevaram, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam; his hymns, as commentators describe them, dwell on the hill's wild creatures, fragrant spices, quiet pools and orchards. Tradition also gathers other holy names around the rock: the sage Agastya, the Siddha Bogar who is said to have meditated here until he attained perfection, and the early king Musukunda Chakravarti. The shrine is held to be many centuries old, an earlier sanctuary having been rebuilt in stone in the Chola age, and worship has continued on the hilltop ever since.
sections.architecture: The temple crowns a small rocky hill and faces east. Pilgrims climb to it by a stairway of roughly five hundred steep, uneven steps cut into the rock, with the green plain opening wider at every turn. The entrance carries a three-tiered gopuram, and accounts describe it as never carried to its full height. In the sanctum the linga of Maragathachaleswarar is of green-toned stone said to shine like an emerald, beneath a three-tiered vimana, while the goddess Marakathavalli, whose name echoes the emerald, is honoured in her own shrine. Figures of Vinayaka and of Murugan with his consorts are described near the entrance arch.
sections.legends: The hill's great legend is cosmic. Vayu, the wind, and Adisesha, the serpent, once contested which was the greater, and Adisesha coiled himself around the mountain while Vayu raised a whirlwind to break his hold. The storm shook fragments of the mountain loose, and they fell in eight places across the land; the one that fell here, tradition says, was an emerald, and it became the Maragatha linga, the Lord of the emerald hill. A second tale explains the name. The sage Agastya came late one evening after worshipping at Kulithalai and Ayyarmalai and found too little daylight left to climb. By his yogic power he became a fly, and so reached the summit; hence the name Eengoimalai, in which the Tamil word for fly is heard.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the major Shaiva observances of the year: Thai Poosam in January or February, Masi Magam in February or March, and the Brahmotsavam in Panguni, in March or April, when the deities are honoured in festival. Maha Shivaratri is especially treasured, and local accounts speak of the sun's rays falling on the presiding deity for a few days around Masi Shivaratri, when the linga is said to change its hue. Monthly Pradosham is observed as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Tiruveengoimalai rewards those who climb. Start early, take the steps slowly, and rest where the stairway opens to a view of the Kaveri plain, the coconut groves and the distant hills. At the top the sanctum is quiet, and the green stone of the Lord is worth a long look before you turn to Marakathavalli in her shrine. The hill has none of the crowds of the great town temples; it is a place for pilgrims who value stillness, birdsong and wind, and the climb itself becomes part of the worship.

visit.timings: Typically open for a morning session and again in the late afternoon into the early evening, with a midday break; sources differ, so confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the foot of the hill. The steps are steep and uneven, so wear comfortable clothing and carry water.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer areas and along the climb but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tiruveengoimalai is about 7 km from Musiri, which lies roughly 43 km from Tiruchirappalli; local buses run from Musiri, and the temple can also be reached from Kulithalai by crossing the Kaveri. Tiruchirappalli Junction is the main railway station, and Tiruchirappalli International Airport, around 50 km away, is the nearest airport. Hire a vehicle for the last stretch if bus timings do not suit.
